The plant is hardy and grows well with minimal care, but applying compost or cow dung manure every 3–4 weeks ensures lush leaves.
Regular weeding is essential.
Since it loves the sun, place the plant in a spot that receives good light.
Pruning the top shoots encourages bushier growth.
harvesting: Gongura is ready to harvest in 45–50 days. Harvest young, tender leaves for the best flavor, as older leaves can become fibrous and less sour. Pluck leaves individually or cut tender branches. Frequent plucking encourages new growth, ensuring a continuous supply for several months.
commonTroubles: Leaf Miners/pCause white trails on leaves; remove affected leaves and spray neem oil.
Aphids/pAttack tender shoots; control with soap water or neem oil spray.
Fungal Leaf Spots/pAppear as dark patches; improve air circulation and avoid overhead watering.

name: Moringa Leaves (Munagaku / Drumstick Leaves)
doYouKnow: Moringa leaves, popularly known as Munagaku in Telugu, are considered a superfood due to their exceptional nutritional value. They are packed with protein, calcium, iron, vitamin C, and antioxidants, making them an excellent addition to daily meals. In India, they are widely used in curries, dals, stir-fries, and powders for health supplements. Regular consumption of moringa leaves is believed to strengthen bones, improve immunity, and reduce fatigue. A simple munagaku pappu or drumstick leaf stir-fry is not just tasty but a true health booster.
varietiesText: Desi Moringa → Traditional variety, commonly grown in Indian backyards, highly nutritious leaves.
PKM-1 Hybrid Moringa → Fast-growing, bushy plant with abundant leaves, ideal for frequent harvest.
Perennial Moringa → Tall, long-living trees producing drumsticks and leaves regularly.

bestCondition.sunlight: Thrives in full sunlight, needing 6–8 hours daily.
bestCondition.water: Requires moderate watering; drought-tolerant once established, but young plants need regular moisture.
bestCondition.soil: Well-drained sandy loam or red soil with good organic matter; pH 6.2–7.0 is ideal.

whenToSow: Moringa can be grown year-round in India, but sowing during the early monsoon (June–July) or early spring (February–March) ensures the best growth.
growingGuide: Moringa is commonly grown from seeds or stem cuttings.
For seeds, sow them directly into the soil about 1 inch deep.
If using cuttings, select a healthy stem about 1–2 feet long and plant it vertically in well-prepared soil.
Ensure regular watering until the plant establishes roots.
Add compost or farmyard manure monthly to boost leaf production.
Prune regularly to prevent the plant from growing too tall and to encourage more side branches for leaf harvest.
Protect young plants from heavy winds, as the stems can be fragile.
harvesting: Leaves can be harvested 6–8 weeks after planting. Pick tender leaflets from branches, leaving enough to allow regrowth. Harvesting can continue year-round. Leaves are best when they are small, tender, and bright green. Avoid old, yellowing leaves as they lose flavor and nutrition. For regular supply, harvest once every 7–10 days.
commonTroubles: Leaf Caterpillars/pChew on leaves; handpick or use neem spray to control.
Aphids and Whiteflies/pAttack tender shoots; treat with soap water or neem oil.
Powdery Mildew/pWhite patches on leaves in humid weather; improve air circulation and spray diluted neem solution.

name: Basil (Tulsi / Sweet Basil)
doYouKnow: Basil, known in India as Tulsi when referring to holy basil and Sweet Basil in culinary use, is both a sacred and medicinal plant. In Indian households, tulsi is worshipped and consumed daily for its healing properties, while sweet basil is popular in continental and fusion cooking, especially in pasta, salads, soups, and herbal teas. Basil is rich in vitamin K, antioxidants, and essential oils that boost immunity, improve digestion, and reduce stress. A cup of fresh basil tea or tulsi water in the morning is considered an age-old remedy for good health.
varietiesText: Holy Basil (Tulsi) → Traditional Indian variety, aromatic leaves, used in teas and Ayurveda.
Sweet Basil → Common in Italian and Thai cooking, tender broad leaves with a sweet aroma.
Thai Basil → Pointed leaves with a hint of spice and licorice flavor, ideal for stir-fries.
Purple Basil → Deep purple leaves, used for garnishing and adding color to salads.

bestCondition.sunlight: Prefers 5–6 hours of direct sunlight daily.
bestCondition.water: Moderate watering; soil should remain moist but not soggy. Avoid waterlogging.
bestCondition.soil: Well-drained loamy soil enriched with compost; thrives in slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6.0–7.0).

whenToSow: Basil is a warm-season crop, best sown from February to June in most parts of India. In southern India, it can be grown almost year-round with proper care.
growingGuide: Sow basil seeds about ¼ inch deep in moist soil. Seeds germinate in 7–10 days.
Once seedlings have 3–4 leaves, thin them to maintain 8–10 inches spacing.
Basil grows well in pots, kitchen gardens, or directly in beds.
Pinch off the top shoots regularly to encourage bushy growth and prevent early flowering.
Adding compost every 2–3 weeks helps keep leaves lush and aromatic.
Avoid overhead watering to prevent fungal issues.
harvesting: Basil is ready to harvest in 35–40 days after sowing. Pluck tender leaves regularly, starting from the top branches. Always leave at least one-third of the plant intact to encourage continuous growth. The best leaves are bright green, soft, and aromatic. Avoid harvesting once flowers bloom, as leaves turn bitter.
commonTroubles: Downy Mildew/pYellowing leaves with gray patches; improve air circulation and avoid wet leaves.
Aphids and Whiteflies/pFound on young shoots; control with neem oil spray.
Root Rot/pCaused by poor drainage and overwatering; use well-drained soil and water moderately.

name: Parsley (Ajmood)
doYouKnow: Parsley, known as Ajmood in Hindi, is a versatile herb used worldwide for garnishing, flavoring, and even for its medicinal benefits. Though not as traditional in Indian cooking as coriander, it’s gaining popularity in salads, soups, pastas, and green juices. Parsley is rich in vitamin C, vitamin K, and iron, making it excellent for blood purification and bone health. Its fresh, slightly peppery flavor can brighten up any dish — from a bowl of soup to a plate of grilled vegetables.
varietiesText: Curly Parsley → Decorative curly leaves, often used for garnishing.
Flat-Leaf Parsley (Italian Parsley) → Stronger flavor, commonly used in cooking.
Hamburg Parsley → Grown for both its leaves and root; roots are used like carrots in stews.

bestCondition.sunlight: Needs 4–6 hours of sunlight; partial shade is also suitable.
bestCondition.water: Requires regular watering; soil should stay moist but not waterlogged.
bestCondition.soil: Fertile, well-drained loamy soil with good compost; prefers pH 6.0–7.0.

whenToSow: Parsley grows best in the cool season (October to February) in India. In cooler hill regions, it can be grown almost year-round.
growingGuide: Soak parsley seeds overnight before sowing to speed up germination, as they are slow to sprout.
Sow seeds about ½ cm deep in moist soil, keeping 6–8 inches spacing.
Germination may take 2–3 weeks.
Thin seedlings to allow enough room for growth.
Regular pruning of outer leaves encourages bushy plants.
Apply compost every 3–4 weeks for lush greenery.
Protect plants from harsh summer heat with shade nets if needed.
harvesting: Parsley is ready to harvest in 70–80 days after sowing. Pick the outer leaves first, leaving the inner shoots to continue growing. Leaves are best when tender, bright green, and fragrant. Avoid harvesting yellowing or tough leaves. Regular harvesting encourages more leaf production.
commonTroubles: Slow Germination/pNormal for parsley; soaking seeds overnight helps.
Aphids/pAttack tender leaves; spray with neem oil or soap water.
Yellowing Leaves/pOften due to nutrient deficiency; add compost or liquid organic fertilizer.

name: Ponaganti Kura (Water Amaranth)
doYouKnow: Ponaganti Kura, also called Water Amaranth, is a traditional leafy green widely grown and consumed in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Known for its ability to thrive in both soil and water-logged areas, it’s a favorite in rural households. Ponaganti is rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins A and C, making it excellent for boosting immunity, improving eyesight, and maintaining strong bones. It is most popularly cooked as a simple stir-fry or dal, often paired with hot rice and ghee for a wholesome meal.
varietiesText: Green-Stem Ponaganti → Tender green leaves with soft stems, mild taste.
Red-Stem Ponaganti → Leaves and stems have a reddish hue; slightly stronger flavor.
Mixed Variety → Combination of red and green leaves, grown in many backyards.

bestCondition.sunlight: Grows well in 5–6 hours of direct sunlight; tolerates partial shade.
bestCondition.water: Thrives in moist or even water-logged soil; regular watering is essential.
bestCondition.soil: Fertile loamy soil enriched with compost; adapts even to marshy or clay soils.

whenToSow: Ponaganti Kura can be grown year-round, but it thrives particularly well during the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons (June to November).
growingGuide: Sow seeds directly into well-prepared soil or sprinkle them in shallow water-logged beds.
Seeds germinate in about 5–7 days.
Thin seedlings to maintain spacing of 6–8 inches between plants.
Since it prefers moisture, ensure regular watering without letting the soil dry out.
Add compost or cow dung manure every 3–4 weeks to encourage lush green leaves.
Regular weeding and pruning of the tops encourage bushier growth and tender leaves.
harvesting: Ponaganti is ready for harvesting in 30–35 days after sowing. Pluck tender leaves and shoots regularly for continuous supply. Leaves should be bright green or reddish (depending on variety) and tender. Avoid over-harvesting from one plant; cut a few stems at a time and allow regrowth.
commonTroubles: Leaf Spot Disease/pBrown patches on leaves; treat with neem-based spray and avoid overhead watering.
Aphids/pAttack tender shoots; spray with soap water or neem oil.
Stunted Growth/pOften due to lack of nutrients; add compost or organic fertilizer.

name: Nalleru (Ceylon Spinach / Basella Alba)
doYouKnow: Nalleru, also called Ceylon Spinach or Basella Alba, is a unique leafy vegetable commonly grown in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Unlike most leafy greens, Nalleru is a climbing vine, with thick, fleshy leaves and stems. It is highly nutritious, rich in iron, calcium, and vitamin C, and is known for its cooling properties. In Andhra cuisine, it is often cooked as a curry, dal, or stir-fry, and sometimes combined with tamarind for a tangy flavor. It also aids digestion and is considered a natural remedy for constipation.
varietiesText: Green-Stem Nalleru → Most common, with thick green stems and leaves; mild taste.
Red-Stem Nalleru → Leaves have a slight reddish tinge; more flavorful and rich in antioxidants.

bestCondition.sunlight: Requires 5–6 hours of direct sunlight daily; partial shade is also tolerated.
bestCondition.water: Needs regular watering; soil should always remain moist as the plant thrives in humidity.
bestCondition.soil: Fertile, well-drained loamy soil enriched with compost; prefers slightly acidic to neutral pH.

whenToSow: Nalleru is a year-round crop in southern India but grows best during the warm, humid months of March to October.
growingGuide: Prepare soil with compost and organic manure.
Sow seeds or plant cuttings directly near a trellis, fence, or stick support, as Nalleru is a climbing vine.
Seeds germinate in 7–10 days.
Provide regular watering and occasional organic fertilizer for vigorous growth.
Mulching helps retain soil moisture.
The plant grows rapidly and can spread widely, so training the vines upwards ensures healthy leaf production.
harvesting: Nalleru is ready for harvesting in 45–50 days after sowing. Tender leaves and young shoots can be plucked every 7–10 days. The leaves should be bright green, thick, and fleshy. Avoid harvesting very old leaves as they may turn fibrous and bitter. Continuous harvesting encourages new vine growth.
commonTroubles: Leaf-Eating Caterpillars/pEat tender leaves; handpick or spray neem solution.

name: Bachali Kura (Malabar Spinach)
doYouKnow: Bachali Kura, also known as Malabar Spinach, is a popular leafy vegetable in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Unlike regular spinach, it is a perennial climbing vine with thick, fleshy leaves that are mildly mucilaginous when cooked. It is an excellent summer green since it thrives in heat and humidity, unlike many other leafy vegetables that wilt during hot weather. Rich in iron, calcium, vitamin A, and folate, Bachali Kura is considered beneficial for improving hemoglobin levels, strengthening bones, and aiding digestion. A traditional favorite is Bachali Kura Pappu (dal) or a curry with sesame and tamarind.
varietiesText: Teega Bachali → The most common variety, with green stems and thick green leaves.
Erra Bachali → Red-stemmed variety, rich in antioxidants, with leaves having a purplish tint.
Local Backyard Varieties → Often grown in village households; highly adaptable and long-yielding.

bestCondition.sunlight: Prefers 6–7 hours of sunlight daily but tolerates partial shade.
bestCondition.water: Requires regular watering; soil should stay moist, as the plant loves humidity.
bestCondition.soil: Fertile, loamy soil enriched with compost or cow dung; thrives best in slightly acidic to neutral soil.

whenToSow: Bachali Kura can be grown almost year-round, but it thrives best during the warm months from March to October. In cooler climates, it slows down in winter.
growingGuide: Sow seeds directly or propagate from stem cuttings near a trellis, fence, or stick for support.
Seeds germinate in 7–10 days.
Since Bachali is a vigorous climber, provide a sturdy support structure.
Water regularly and apply compost or vermicompost every 3–4 weeks to promote lush growth.
Prune the vines regularly to control length and encourage side shoots.
Avoid letting the plant flower too early, as leaf production reduces after flowering.
harvesting: Leaves can be harvested in 40–45 days after sowing. Pluck young leaves and tender shoots regularly. Always harvest from the top and sides to allow continuous regrowth. Leaves should be thick, glossy, and bright green (or purplish for red-stemmed varieties). Avoid harvesting very mature leaves as they can become fibrous and less tasty.

name: Chukka Kura (Sorrel Leaves / Rumex Vesicarius)
doYouKnow: Chukka Kura, also known as Sorrel Leaves, is a tangy leafy vegetable that adds a refreshing sour flavor to many Andhra-style dishes. Unlike Gongura, which has a sharp sourness, Chukka Kura has a milder tang, making it perfect for quick curries, dals, and chutneys. It is rich in iron, vitamin C, and folic acid, making it excellent for improving blood health, boosting immunity, and aiding digestion. A popular preparation is Chukka Kura Pappu, a comforting dish paired with hot rice and ghee.
varietiesText: Desi Green Chukka Kura → Common variety with tender green leaves and mild tang.
Broad-Leaf Chukka Kura → Larger leaves, used for quick curries and chutneys.

bestCondition.sunlight: Requires 5–6 hours of sunlight daily; partial shade is tolerated.
bestCondition.water: Needs regular watering; soil should be kept moist but not waterlogged.
bestCondition.soil: Grows best in sandy loam soil enriched with organic compost; prefers a slightly acidic soil.

whenToSow: Chukka Kura can be grown throughout the year, but thrives best during the cooler months of September to February.
growingGuide: Seeds are usually sown directly into well-prepared soil beds. Sow them about ½ inch deep and 6 inches apart.
Germination takes 6–8 days.
Keep the soil moist and weed-free.
Apply compost or organic fertilizer every 3–4 weeks to boost leaf growth.
Since the plant grows low to the ground, keep the beds clean and dry to prevent fungal infections.
Regular pruning of leaves helps continuous growth.
harvesting: Leaves can be harvested in 25–30 days after sowing. Pluck tender leaves regularly, as younger leaves have the best flavor and texture. Harvesting outer leaves while leaving the inner ones ensures a longer harvesting period. Avoid letting the plant flower, as leaf production reduces afterward.

name: Spring Onion (Green Onion / Scallion)
doYouKnow: Spring Onion, also called Green Onion or Scallion, is a versatile vegetable used both for its long green leaves and tender white bulbs. In Indian cooking, it is often added to stir-fries, noodles, parathas, and curries for its mild onion flavor. Rich in vitamin C, vitamin K, and antioxidants, spring onions help boost immunity, improve bone health, and aid digestion. They are also very quick-growing, making them a favorite in kitchen gardens. Freshly harvested spring onions give a crisp texture and a delicate flavor that enhances any dish.
varietiesText: White Lisbon → Popular variety with long, tender stalks and mild flavor.
Evergreen Bunching → Perennial type that regrows after cutting, perfect for continuous harvest.
Local Desi Varieties → Grown widely in Indian backyards, adaptable to different climates.

bestCondition.sunlight: Needs 5–6 hours of direct sunlight daily.
bestCondition.water: Requires moderate watering; soil should be moist but not waterlogged.
bestCondition.soil: Loose, sandy loam soil rich in organic matter; prefers slightly acidic to neutral pH (6.0–7.0).

whenToSow: Spring Onions can be grown almost year-round, but the best seasons are October to February for the best yield and quality.
growingGuide: Spring onions can be grown from seeds or sets (small bulbs). Sow seeds ½ inch deep in rows 6 inches apart.
Thin seedlings after germination to avoid crowding.
Regular watering is essential, especially during dry spells, to keep the bulbs tender and juicy.
Adding compost every 2–3 weeks ensures steady growth.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizers, as they can make the stalks floppy.
For kitchen gardening, spring onions also grow well in pots and containers.
harvesting: Spring onions are ready to harvest in 45–55 days after sowing. Pull out the whole plant when bulbs are ½ to 1 inch thick, or cut the green tops as needed for continuous supply. The best harvest is when the stalks are crisp, green, and upright. Avoid waiting too long, as older stalks become fibrous and lose flavor.
commonTroubles: Onion Thrips/pTiny pests that damage leaves; spray neem oil or garlic extract solution.
